case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: The holding is about the CFAA only. It leaves contract, trespass to chattels, copyright and state privacy claims fully available, and LinkedIn later prevailed on contract grounds.
case.holding: Scraping data that a website makes publicly available without any login does not amount to access without authorisation under the CFAA.
case.case_name: hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp.

case.why_ai_cites_it: The principal authority that collecting public web data is not a federal computer crime, which is the first hurdle any web-scale training corpus has to clear.

reading.body:
The Ninth Circuit held in 2022 that scraping publicly available website data without login credentials does not violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, removing the primary federal barrier to large-scale data collection.

This holding matters because web-scale AI training depends on assembling billions of examples from public sources. The CFAA had been read by some courts to prohibit any access a website owner dislikes, which would have criminalized the basic infrastructure of modern language models. The hiQ decision clarified that public data remains public under federal computer crime law.

The ruling is narrow. It addresses only the CFAA. LinkedIn later won its case against hiQ on other grounds, particularly contract law. Copyright, state privacy statutes, and trespass to chattels remain available to website operators who wish to prevent scraping. The decision tells you what federal computer crime law permits, not what else might restrict data collection.

This decision does not resolve whether scrapers need the computational resources to do so at scale, nor whether power and cooling constraints will eventually matter more than legal ones. It clears one legal hurdle for training infrastructure. The binding constraints on data collection may come from physics and grid capacity rather than courtrooms.
